04Designing and refining the reporting experience

From an emergency form to a problem report people trust

The first iteration put the new IA into a step-by-step form. Testing showed where language, privacy, and tracking still got in the way.

Iteration 1 · Sprint 3

The first redesigned form

A short, guided flow: say where the problem is, choose what it is, optionally add details and contact information, review, and get a ticket to track.

01
Landing page

Detailed instructions for how to get started.

02
Problem category

An easy point of entry based on where the problem occurred, with the option to select “Other.”

03
Sub-category: Outdoors

Common problem types based on the location of the issue.

04
Problem details

An optional opportunity to add a photo, suggested tags, and a description.

05
Review

The ability to correct information before submitting.

The contact information and tracking screens from this iteration are shown in the comparisons below.

Usability testing · Sprint 3

What testing the first iteration showed

Wins
  • The form met user expectations and was understandable and easy to use.
  • Most participants added their contact information and agreed to receive alerts.
  • Users appreciated being able to add tags to give their issue more context.
  • Participants found the ticket tracking process helpful.
  • Users appreciated being able to review and edit their information before submitting.
4.6 / 5average confidence score
Opportunities
  • “Emergency” language may cause hesitancy to fill out the form.
  • Ticket status: users wanted to be reminded of what they submitted.
  • Data privacy: some worried their contact information or data could be used to send unrelated alerts later.
  • Users were initially unsure how to categorize a problem that could fit several categories.
  • There was no option to choose a notification preference.
  • Users wanted to add a comment after submitting the form.
  • Most users couldn't think of a scenario where they'd use “Other” for a problem that is neither indoors nor outdoors.
Sprint 4 design challenge

Sprint 4 goals

As facilitator of Sprint 4, I directed the course of the project, oversaw the schedule, and led client presentations. The sprint set four goals:

01
Update the web form to incorporate findings and recommendations from user testing
Design decisions below →
02
Design a customer service form to redirect miscellaneous issues such as billing inquiries
Customer Service form →
03
Hand off deliverables to developers and collaborate with them regularly, so the final product represents both users' and DC Water's needs
Outcomes →
04
Design an artificial intelligence application that gives users an alternative, more efficient way to report a problem
Photo-based reporting →
Iteration 2 · Sprint 4

Design decisions in the second iteration

We updated the web form based on the testing results. Each change below traces from a finding to the redesign.

Terminology: from “Report an Emergency” to “Report a Problem”

What we learned

“Emergency” language may make people hesitate, and earlier testing showed users weren't sure their issue was a true emergency.

↓
What changed

The form title changed from “Report an Emergency” to “Report a Problem,” to make users less likely to abandon the form when they aren't sure their issue is a true emergency.

Before · Iteration 1
After · Iteration 2

Notifications: preferences and clearer consent

What we learned

There was no way to choose a notification preference, and some participants worried their data could be used for unrelated alerts.

↓
What changed

A simpler, more concise contact form with notification preferences. Receiving updates was separated from allowing DC Water to make contact, and the screen states that DC Water will only contact the user about this ticket.

Before · Iteration 1

One yes/no question about status alerts.

After · Iteration 2

Updates and contact permissions chosen separately, by phone call or email.

Ticket tracking: show what was submitted

What we learned

Participants found ticket tracking helpful but wanted to be reminded of what they had submitted.

↓
What changed

The ticket status page was redesigned to show the ticket's status and a new “Ticket Details” tab with the submitted information. An option to rate the experience and leave feedback was also added.

Before · Iteration 1

Current status and generalized next steps.

After · Iteration 2

Case History and Ticket Details tabs, plus rating and feedback.

Categories: fewer choices up front, a clear route when unsure

What we learned

Users were unsure how to categorize problems that fit several categories, and most couldn't imagine using “Other” for a problem that was neither indoors nor outdoors.

↓
What the final screens show

“Where is the problem?” offers only Outdoors and Indoors, with a link to describe the issue if unsure. “Other / Not Sure” moves to the problem-type step. The final flow also starts with a location step.

Before · Iteration 1

Outdoors, Indoors, Other.

Final

Outdoors and Indoors, with a link for anyone who's unsure.

Customer Service form · Sprint 4

Separating problems from inquiries

DC Water's previous form combined emergency issues and miscellaneous inquiries in one form, which confused users. We decided to direct people to two different forms based on their issue or inquiry, and designed a new Customer Service form for miscellaneous issues such as billing inquiries.

First, we worked with DC Water to decide which options could be left out of the new form because they were covered elsewhere on its website.
